entities.summary:
Parkinson's Law is a timeless adage that describes how work expands to fill the time available for its completion. Created by C. Northcote Parkinson in the mid-20th century, this concept has far-reaching implications for organizational management and productivity. By understanding the psychological and behavioral factors that contribute to Parkinson's Law, individuals can develop strategies to overcome procrastination and achieve more efficiency in their work.

Parkinson's Law is rooted in the observation that as time becomes available, an individual's workload tends to increase proportionally. This phenomenon has been observed in various contexts, from office environments to large corporations, and even within governments. The law suggests that the mere availability of resources or freedom can lead to a decrease in productivity.

The significance of Parkinson's Law lies in its ability to explain a common human experience: the tendency to procrastinate when faced with tasks of varying complexity. By recognizing this pattern, individuals can take proactive steps to manage their time more effectively and improve their overall work performance.

As a cultural phenomenon, Parkinson's Law has been referenced and discussed in various fields, including psychology, sociology, and business studies. It continues to inspire research and debate among scholars and practitioners alike, highlighting the importance of understanding human behavior in organizational settings.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "Parkinson's Law is a satirical adage and a book (full title: Parkinson's Law, or The Pursuit of Progress) by the British historian, naval historian, and management satirist C. Northcote Parkinson (1909–1993), derived from an essay first published in The Economist on 19 November 1955 and expanded into a book published by Houghton Mifflin in 1958. Parkinson's Law states: 'Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.' The essay and book argue, through mock-scholarly historical analysis of the British Admiralty and Colonial Office, that the number of officials in any bureaucracy tends to increase at a fixed annual rate (5.17% to 6.56% per year, Parkinson claims with satirical statistical precision), regardless of the actual work to be done — bureaucratic expansion is self-perpetuating, driven by two motivating factors: the desire of officials to multiply their subordinates (rather than their rivals), and the tendency for officials to create work for each other.

Parkinson's Law is one of the most widely cited aphorisms in management theory and organisational science — its formulation of the tendency of bureaucratic expansion to outpace productive need has been verified by empirical research and applied to fields ranging from government administration through software development (in Scrum and Agile methodologies, where Parkinson's Law is cited as a reason for time-boxing tasks) to personal productivity (in time management, where the principle suggests that deadlines should be set aggressively to prevent work from expanding).

Parkinson's corollary laws — 'Expenditure rises to meet income', 'Delay is the deadliest form of denial', and 'Officials want to multiply subordinates, not rivals' — have similarly entered the lexicon of management theory.
